summary: Defines the Network Control Protocol for setting up and configuring DECnet Phase IV routing over PPP. It does not cover other protocols such as MOP or LAT. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The rules for a link to say hello and agree to carry one old company's network traffic.

questions: how does decnet run over ppp
subtitle: How a PPP link agrees to carry DECnet Phase IV routing traffic, treating the serial line like an Ethernet.

tldr.problem: A router running DNA Phase IV Routing (DECnet Phase IV) needs a standard way to switch that protocol on over a PPP link, and to put its packets into PPP frames.
tldr.mechanism: DNCP reuses the LCP packet exchange (Codes 1 through 7, no options) to open and close the routing protocol, and routing packets travel in PPP frames with a two-octet length prefix and Ethernet-style contents.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1376. It covers only DNA Phase IV Routing, not other DNA protocols such as MOP or LAT.

today: RFC 1762 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1376. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Two Ways to Run DECnet over a Serial Line
sections.content:
RFC 1762 defines the Network Control Protocol (NCP) that sets up Digital's DNA Phase IV Routing protocol (DECnet Phase IV) over the Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP). PPP itself, defined in RFC 1661, provides a standard way to encapsulate network-layer traffic over point-to-point links and proposes a family of NCPs for configuring each network-layer protocol.

The RFC names two basic approaches for running Phase IV Routing over a serial line. Several router vendors treat the serial link as an Ethernet and use the same data and control messages an Ethernet would use. Digital's own approach uses DDCMP and slightly different control messages. This document defines a method that uses the first approach.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to send these messages down a wire. This document picks the one that pretends the wire is a normal office network cable.

sections.title: Which Phase IV Protocols Are Covered
sections.content:
The RFC lists the Phase IV DNA protocols that act as data link clients: Routing, System Console, Digital Customer Use, Diagnostics, the Naming Service (DNS), the Time Service (DTS), Load/Dump, Experimental Use, Communications Test and Digital Protocol X1. Each gets a short description.

Only the first is in scope. The document applies to DNA Phase IV Routing messages, both data and control, and not to other DNA Phase IV protocols such as MOP and LAT. The Routing protocol is described as a network layer protocol providing services similar to those of DoD IP: it routes messages in Phase IV DECnet networks and manages the packet flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The company had many kinds of network messages. This document only handles the one that works like a postal sorting system, and leaves the rest alone.

sections.title: The DNA Phase IV Routing Control Protocol
sections.content:
The DNA Phase IV Routing Control Protocol (DNCP) configures, enables and disables the Phase IV Routing modules on both ends of the link. It uses the same packet exchange mechanism as the Link Control Protocol (LCP) and is exactly the same as LCP except for a few listed differences.

  • DNCP packets may not be exchanged until PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase. Packets received before then should be silently discarded.
  • Exactly one DNCP packet goes in the Information field of a PPP frame whose Protocol field is hex 8027.
  • Only Codes 1 through 7 are used: Configure-Request, Configure-Ack, Configure-Nak, Configure-Reject, Terminate-Request, Terminate-Ack and Code-Reject. Other Codes are treated as unrecognized and should result in Code-Rejects.
  • DNCP has no Configuration Options.

On timeouts, an implementation should be prepared to wait for Authentication and Link Quality Determination to finish before timing out on a Configure-Ack or other response. It is suggested that an implementation give up only after user intervention or a configurable amount of time.
sections.plainLanguage: The two machines use the same polite hello and goodbye steps they already use for the wire itself. There is nothing to bargain over here, just a yes or a no to turn the service on.

sections.title: Sending Routing Packets in PPP Frames
sections.content:
Before any Routing packets are sent, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and DNCP must reach the Opened state.

Each PPP frame then carries exactly one length field and one Routing packet, with the Protocol field set to hex 0027. The length field counts the octets of the Routing packet. It is two octets long and is stored in VAX byte ordering, least significant byte first, to match DNA Phase IV Routing over Ethernet. It is needed to tell optional padding octets from real information.

The Routing packet itself has the same format as over Ethernet, without the Ethernet header, Pad and FCS fields. Its maximum length is the maximum length of the PPP Information field minus 2 octets for the length field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets a small label at the front saying how long it is, so the receiver can tell real message from empty padding at the end.

sections.title: Routing Timers and Endnodes
sections.content:
When the network topology changes, Phase IV Routing nodes propagate the change at once through Level 1 and Level 2 Routing messages, with a 1 second minimum delay between updates. They also periodically resend the complete Level 1 and Level 2 distance vectors to guard against corrupted host memory and, on Ethernet, packet loss.

Digital's serial links use DDCMP, which guarantees delivery, so the recommended default retransmit time there is long (600 seconds). Ethernet does not guarantee delivery, so its recommended default is short (10 seconds). Because PPP sits between these cases, the RFC recommends that the time between routing updates be user configurable per PPP interface, based on the error rate of the underlying data link.

The Hello timer and Listen timer should follow the broadcast link recommendations, 15 and 45 seconds. Routers MAY skip sending routing updates when the remote node is an endnode, and endnodes MUST discard all routing updates received over a PPP link. A node's type can be learned from the hello messages it sends.
sections.plainLanguage: Machines repeat their route lists every so often in case something got lost. On a wire that never loses anything they can repeat rarely; on a shakier wire, more often. Machines that only receive mail, and do not pass it on, ignore the route lists.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC contains a Security Considerations section, but it says only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. Authentication, where used, happens in an earlier PPP phase before DNCP packets may be exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not talk about how to keep bad guys out. It only describes how to turn the service on.
